topic: RBI Plans Trial of Polymer (Plastic) Currency Notes

subtopics.title: Polymer Banknotes: Concept and Proposal
subtopics.summary: Polymer banknotes are printed on a specialised plastic substrate, primarily BOPP, instead of cotton-based banknote paper. RBI has revived a proposal for such notes that was first made in 2009, and BRBNMPL invited global bids for the polymer substrate. Australia was the first country to introduce a complete series of polymer banknotes, in 1988.
facts: Polymer banknotes use a specialised plastic substrate, primarily BOPP.
BOPP stands for Biaxially Oriented Polypropylene.
Polymer notes replace conventional cotton-based banknote paper.
Australia was the first country to introduce a complete series of polymer banknotes, in 1988.
The initial proposal for polymer notes in India dates to 2009.
RBI revived the proposal to introduce durable polymer-based banknotes.
RBI invited bids to procure polymer notes in the current initiative.
BRBNMPL, RBI's note-printing subsidiary, invited global bids for a BOPP-based polymer substrate.
BRBNMPL was established in 1995 in Bengaluru.

subtopics.title: Advantages of Polymer Notes
subtopics.summary: Polymer notes are more resistant to tearing, less vulnerable to water and moisture, and more durable under frequent circulation. They can carry advanced anti-counterfeiting features that are much harder to replicate than on paper. Because individual notes last longer, fewer new notes need to be manufactured to keep supply steady.

More durable under frequent circulation.
Capable of incorporating advanced anti-counterfeiting features.
Polymer notes remain usable for significantly longer periods.
Longer life means less frequent replacement cycles.

Less frequent replacement lowers the long-term environmental footprint.

subtopics.title: Costs, Supply Chain and Environmental Challenges
subtopics.summary: Polymer notes cost significantly more to produce than paper currency, and their production cost is tied to global oil prices. The notes are made from polypropylene, and reliance on imported polypropylene creates import dependency. Plastic waste needs a specialised collection and recycling system, and the transition requires changes to ATMs, vending machines and cash-handling machines.
facts: Polymer notes cost significantly more to produce than conventional paper currency.
Production cost is tied to global oil prices.
Polymer notes are made from polypropylene.
Reliance on imported polypropylene creates import dependency.

subtopics.title: Currency Management and Printing in India
subtopics.summary: Currency and coinage fall under the Union List, and the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934 provides the principal legal framework for issuing banknotes. RBI issues notes, estimates currency requirements and ensures circulation of good-quality notes. SPMCIL and BRBNMPL together operate four presses that print all banknotes in India.
facts: Currency, coinage, legal tender and foreign exchange fall within the Union List.
Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934 is the principal legal framework for issuing banknotes.
Coinage Act, 2011 deals with the design, production and minting, and circulation of coins.
RBI roles include issuing banknotes and estimating the country's currency requirements.
Four currency printing presses print all banknotes of India.
SPMCIL is a Government of India enterprise operating 2 presses, including one at Nashik, Maharashtra.
BRBNMPL is a wholly owned RBI subsidiary operating 2 presses, at Mysuru (Karnataka) and Salboni (West Bengal).
Bank Note Paper Mill India Pvt. Ltd. manufactures banknote paper domestically.
RBI introduced the Clean Note Policy in 1999.
Government designs and mints coins, and RBI distributes them through its currency management network.

quizzes.passage: The Reserve Bank of India has revived a proposal to introduce polymer-based banknotes in India. Polymer currency notes are manufactured using a specialised plastic substrate, primarily Biaxially Oriented Polypropylene, instead of conventional cotton-based banknote paper. The idea is not new, as an initial proposal was made in 2009. Bharatiya Reserve Bank Note Mudran Private Limited, a wholly owned subsidiary of the RBI, has invited global bids for a BOPP-based polymer substrate to manufacture polymer banknotes. Banknotes in India are printed at four currency printing presses, and together they print all the banknotes of India in different denominations. Under the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934, the RBI issues banknotes, estimates the country's currency requirements and maintains an adequate supply of banknotes. The Government of India, on the other hand, approves the design and material of banknotes based on recommendations of the RBI's Central Board. Coins are minted under the Coinage Act, 2011, and are then supplied to the RBI, which distributes them to banks and the public. The RBI has also introduced a Clean Note Policy so that the public receives currency notes and coins of acceptable quality. Currency, coinage, legal tender and foreign exchange fall within the legislative domain of the Union Government under the Union List.

Coins are supplied to the RBI after minting, and the RBI distributes them through its currency management network to banks and the public.
